utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, ladies and gentlemen. Good morning to the technicians. Good morning to the interpreters. We should resume our hearings. Mr. Dubuisson, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case, IT-95-14/1-T, the Prosecutor versus Zlatko Aleksovski.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Today, as yesterday, may we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution. Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, please. My name is Niemann and I appear with my colleagues, Mr. Meddegoda and Ms. Sutherland for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Niemann. And for the Defence, please, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Mikulicic and I appear with my colleague, Mr. Joka for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, then. All your names are down on the transcript, we may now proceed. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours, the Defence calls witness, Anto Pesa. (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pesa. Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now take the oath. The usher is holding the text out for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please take your seat. Do you feel comfortable, Mr. Pesa?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well then. To begin with, you will please answer the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic, the gentleman on your left. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pesa. In this hearing I represent the interests of the Defence. In that sense I am going to ask you several questions, which I should like to ask you to answer to the best of your ability. Tell us, please, Mr. Pesa, when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I was born on the 27th of May, 1948, in the Village of Orasac of the Municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What nationality are you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a religious person?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Of which faith?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: The Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pesa, did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Eight years of school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you completed primary school where?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: In Han Bila, four classes and then up by Vuca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Pesa, that you were born in the Village of Orasac. How far is that village away from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: About 20 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you lived there since your birth?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, I was born there and lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you live in your own house or in an apartment building with other neighbours?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, I had my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you got a family?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, whether you have any children?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many children have you got?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I have six children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us how old they are and what sex?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Three sons and three daughters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You all lived in your house in Orasac at the beginning of 1993 or not?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, I have been living there all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Together with your family; that's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, and with my mother.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: With your mother, yes. And with your wife, I suppose?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, my wife, my mother and my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you employed or were you a farmer?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, I was employed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you work?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: In Nova Bila, in Sebesce.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the work you did?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: For a time I was a worker, unskilled worker. And then I passed some exams and became a skilled worker and worked with machines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So along with the work you did, you qualified for a better job?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, I was given a better machine to work with and a higher wage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Pesa, that in the first half of 1993, together with your family, you had to leave your house, the house you had lived in up until then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why did you have to leave your home?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: We had to leave because there was an attack in the first half of 1993 by the BH Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say that the BH Army attacked, did it attack your village or your house?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: It attacked the whole population of the Croat population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you were forced to flee and to leave that area as a refugee?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Together with your family?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: We went to Nova Bila, across the hill with my children, with my wife, and with my mother who was born in 1920. My mother at that time was in very poor health and I had to take care of her because she was old. I came to Nova Bila and I then thought about what I was going to do. I found some kind of transport. I can't remember exactly. It was a tractor. And I went to Busovaca. And I went to contact the Red Cross there. However, on that occasion, the Red Cross lodged me in a private house, and when I came there, the house was empty. I live there today. It was a very run down house. It was dirty, but that was what the times were like. We had to have a roof over our heads and that is where I live to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you live in Busovaca today, you've been living there since mid-1993; is that correct, is your family there with you as well?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesa, at that time in the area of Busovaca, there were conflicts between the Muslim and Croatian population. Do you recall those events?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Pesa, you mentioned in your introduction that you have three sons. How old are your sons? How old were your sons at that time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: One was 1968, born in 1968, one was born in 1970 and the third in 1972.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, if my calculations are correct, all three sons were of an age when they were, in fact, conscripts?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did your sons do when they came to Busovaca with you? Did they go to contact the HVO or did they stay at home?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I and my sons were members of the HVO. While I lived in Orasac and when I came to Busovaca we were also members of the HVO and they went to the defence department there to give their names, and they would distribute them and assign them to various areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where were they assigned to, armed formations or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, armed formations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Pesa, whether you went to the defence department as well?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I am a conscript until the age of 65 and I, therefore, considered, I wondered what I could do to help and that is why I went to the department. When my sons went, I went with them to give my name and say that I was able and willing to help. And then the gentleman there would decide what I was able to do. I got my war assignment. I was in the civilian protection department for work operations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, as a conscript, you were not sent to the armed forces, but were sent to a work unit in Busovaca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Pesa, what was your duty as a member of the work unit?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, for example, when a courier would bring in a request for me to contact people and to go to dig dugouts, trenches, fox holes and so on and that is what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, a courier would be sent to your home and he would then tell you to go and contact your superiors for you to carry out your duties. Where did you go then?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, I would go trench digging in Busovaca. I was a refugee in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Perhaps you did not understand me. Where did you go? Where was the meeting point that you were to go to?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: It was by the secondary school in Busovaca. I was told to go to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That was the meeting point for other individuals who had been called up and who were members of that work unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many people, approximately, worked in your work unit?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Every time that we would gather, there were about 15 to 20 of us at the collection point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pesa, when you would meet in front of the school in Busovaca, then I suppose you would go on location; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you go to the location you were assigned to and were you accompanied by anybody?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: We were accompanied by the military police and we were taken by a truck, a tractor, or transport of that kind, as far as it was able to go. Then when tractors and cars were no longer able to pass, then we would carry on on foot and take up our work duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you would gather in Busovaca, the military police would then escort you to the locality in which you were to perform your work and who would you contact there?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, it was the commander of the line, frontline. That's the particular sector that I was sent to. We would report to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What would happen then? Who would say exactly what spot you were to work on and what you were to do?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, the commander would send us there to dig trenches, dugouts, communicating trenches, fox holes and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. And then you went out to do your work, is that so?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What tools did you use?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Picks and axes and shovels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you take the tools with you from your home or were you handed these tools to work with?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, they were given out to us by the work unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesa, tell us, please, what kind of work you did most often?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, I dug. I dug trenches mostly. And the dugouts and the fox holes and that was our work duty, digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These communicating trenches and dugouts and fox holes, were they for the purposes of the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall, Mr. Pesa, how many times you, yourself, in the course of 1993, were taken to do digging, to dig trenches, how many times were you taken out to do this kind of work?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: It depended on requirements, but if I were to add them up, I would say twice a week, sometimes every night. Sometimes we would have a break. Depending on the needs. I can't tell you exactly how many times throughout that time, but I did go frequently. I can't remember the exact number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, and a lot of time has gone by as well. Mr. Pesa, you said that in one shift of the work unit, there would be about 15 to 20 individuals depending on the occasion, do you remember the ethnic composition of the people who worked with you in these work units? The people digging the trenches?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well as far as I know they were mostly Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were these other people also from Busovaca or were they from the environs? Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, I was a refugee, so I don't know where the other people were from, whether they were refugees like me whom I knew from the neighbouring municipalities and villages. But I suppose there were some locals as well. I didn't know the locals because I was a refugee myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember the locations that you did this digging? Can you enumerate them for us, please?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes. In Prosje, in Kula, in Krcrvine, Loncari, Komarevo and Polom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You gave us these names a little too quickly. Could you repeat the names of the places once again. I am not sure that everything was entered into the transcript. Could you repeat the localities, please, a little more slowly?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I dug trenches, dugouts and so on in Kula, in Prosje, in Komarevo, Loncari and I forget one more place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said Polom.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: And perhaps some other localities as well. It was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When I asked you what nationality the people who dug trenches with you, you said that they were predominantly Croats. How did you come to conclude that they were Croats? How do you know they were Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, when we came there, I thought they were all Croats. I didn't know them all, of course. I said that I thought they were Croats. Perhaps there were some Muslims. Perhaps there were some Serbs. But I didn't know the people personally, but I considered that they were Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So it was your supposition that they were Croats?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the localities where you did the digging. Can you tell us, I know that you're not from the region, you're a refugee, but perhaps in the meantime you got to know the area better, could you tell us in comparison to Busovaca, where are these localities? Are they near Busovaca? Are they further away from Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: They are all near Busovaca. These localities are not in town. They are the environs of Busovaca. For example, given that Prosje is up above, slightly up above Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, very well, these are all places around Busovaca. Tell us, please, Mr. Pesa, do you know why you were sent to dig trenches? What were those trenches used for, do you know?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, they were dug for purposes of self-defence because Busovaca was attacked by the BH Army. So it was for purposes of self-protection, to protect the people. To protect the soldiers. So it was war, and it was for self-protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Tell us, please, while you were working in these localities, were they along the frontlines or were they a little further away?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, they were along the frontline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that near these localities, the BH Army was located?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, up in Prosje, for example, I remember this, along the frontline, everybody was along the frontlines. And I personally saw that the BH Army was not more than 100 metres away from us. And when we dug these trenches during the night and when the picks and shovels hit the ground in the process of digging, it's night, it's very silent, and I think that this BH Army could hear us digging and they would then open fire on us. So our commanders would say, you have to dig quietly so they can't hear the digging and don't attack you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesa, you said that you were told to work silently, who would tell you to do this?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, the military police would tell us, our escort, the military police would tell us to dig quietly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that while you were in those localities, the military police was there to ensure your safety; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pesa, if there was any more gun fire from the side of the BH Army, which was very close to where you were digging as you said, if there was any greater firing, what would the military police do? Would it protect you in some way? Would it escort you away from this locality?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, we were informed that if there was more shelling that we would be withdrawn to the rear because we were civilians, we did not have any arms. All we had were our tools to dig the trenches. And we were told that if there was any gun fire, we would be withdrawn to the rear because we had nothing to counter these attacks. All we had were tools.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And did that ever happen that you were withdrawn to the rear?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, when we did some digging near Pula, I can't remember the date, it was 3.15 at night. This was very, there was a lot of fighting and there were 17 of us at that time, and it was all we could do to withdraw quick enough because it was a strong attack. But we, we would retreat, some others remained up in the locality to protect us. They were the military police and they remained up at the front line. But we were civilians, and that is why we retreated. That is one of the incidents that I personally had occasion to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pesa, you mentioned on several occasions that you went out digging at night. Did you always dig during the night or did you do your digging in the day as well?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, only at night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For how long did one shift of this digging go on?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: We would start working when night would fall, and we would go on working until daybreak, until dawn. And as soon as the day would start we would withdraw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, up there where you worked, where you were digging, did you get food?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who brought your food?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Food was brought in to us by the army. I mean, those people who were in charge of the military police. We got food together with them, food and water.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did you get some special food or did you eat the same food that the soldiers ate?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: The same food, nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there enough food?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, to tell you the truth, no. There simply wasn't enough food, you see, we ate food like everyone else, but we were surrounded. It is not that we could receive supplies from somewhere. For example, there was canned fish or, I don't know, they would cook beans, or something would be brought in, invariably; but it wasn't that it was high quality food, but it kept us going.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. But the way it was in your case, that is the way it was for everyone; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned that there was not enough food because you were surrounded. What did you mean by that? When you were digging were you surrounded, or was Busovaca surrounded?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I think that we were surrounded, I mean all of us in central Bosnia were surrounded, all of us. So, we did not have communication lines open so we could get things, buy things, so we could get better food. So, I'm talking about central Bosnia in the Lasva Valley, all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. Tell us, Mr. Pesa, did you personally have some kind of an accident while you were working there? Did something happen to you?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, I was wounded while we were carrying out this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can you describe how this happened?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: During the first half of 1993 I went out to work near Krcevine at a place called Milavci and I was digging trenches up there. I was working and I stepped on a mine, it's a special kind of mine, and it blew my leg off, and I still wear a prosthesis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, as you were working up there you were wounded by a mine; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And on that occasion you were wounded and you were taken to a hospital; right? Where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I was taken to the outpatient clinic in Busovaca. I mean, there wasn't even medicine or anything, just so the bleeding would stop. I was taken to Nova Bila hospital, but we had to take a round road. So I was put there, I don't know whether you're going to understand this, I mean, we were actually put on church pews, we actually laid on pews. We would put pews together like those from a church, and that is where we would sleep. I lay there on this wooden bench, like a pew in a church, and there was nothing, there weren't any injections or pills or any medicine, nothing. So, I spent there as long as I was there. I mean, a month or whatever, then I was taken to Croatia, to Split. And then they really amputated, they cut off my leg, or whatever, and that is how it all ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So now you're a disabled person; right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What percentage?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Seventy per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Pesa, you were born in the village of Orasac and that is where your house and property were, and you had to escape from there when the BH army attacked. After you fled from this area, did you have an opportunity to go and see your house?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was it like?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, you know, UNPROFOR was up there in Busovaca and they gave us newspapers to read, and I talked to a translator there and I heard about this freedom of movement. And I said, "Well, if there is freedom of movement, does that include me, too? Can I go and see my native village and my house?" However, a few times I would repeat that, you know, when they were distributing these newspapers down by the marketplace and all that, and I saw that nobody responded. The UNPROFOR man who was on an APC, he called my name out and I went with him to Tisa Busovaca, and then I saw another translator there, a person called Zoran from Bugojno and explained what I was looking for and what I was interested in, in this freedom of movement, could I see my house. And he said no problem. We went there, I can't tell you what date, I went there under their protection, but that was this freedom of movement, on APCs, you know. I got into the village, and when I got into the village there was some foreign army out there. I mean, we called them the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say a foreign army, the Mujahedin, who are these persons, are they citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina or someone else?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, they are not citizens of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, they are Arabs. I don't know why we call them the Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: They were in your village?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What about your house and your land?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, on my land they built some kind of religious building. I don't know, about 35 metres wide and 25 metres long, and there was water there for their hygiene. And then on the second floor they carried out religious rights, and I don't know, they had offices up there or something, I don't know. And this building is in this village of mine to the present day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're not allowed to stay in your home?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, no, not only in my case, but everything in the village was destroyed and burned down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. So, if I'm not mistaken, until the present day you are a refugee in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just one more question, Mr. Pesa. You said that when you were supposed to go out and work, a messenger would come and tell you that you were supposed to go out there; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, did the military police ever come to pick you up rather than a messenger?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, yeah, yeah. I mean, it's not that I was forced to go up there, you know. If I wasn't at home, yes, the military police would tell my wife and they would tell me I was supposed to go there. But most of the time it was a messenger who would come rather than the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Pesa, do you perhaps know whether there were some neighbours of yours, or someone else, who did not want to respond to this kind of call up for work duty?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, sir, to tell you the truth, I was only interested in myself and my own family and I took care of them, and I'm not aware of anything of that sort.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Pesa, in these moments when you worked on the ground, did you ever see some Muslims working next to you or near you, Muslims who were interned in the Kaonik facility?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you personally ever in Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps get to know the warden of Kaonik?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know a person called Zlatko Aleksovski?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Pesa the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Meddegoda, I believe you are the one to put the questions to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pesa. I will be putting a few questions to you on behalf of the Prosecution, and I would appreciate if you could answer them to the best of your knowledge and the best of your recollection. Mr. Pesa, in answer to my learned colleague, you said you were forced to leave your village of Orasac in the first half of 1993, in mid-1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Do you remember about which month of 1993 that you left the village of Orasac?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, no, I know it was the first half, but I don't know which month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Was it January of 1993 that you had to leave or was it later?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't remember. I know it was the first half, but I don't know the date, I've had so many problems how could I know what month it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you, together with the family, moved on to Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where did you report to? You said you reported, you and your sons, reported to the defence department?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Where did you report? To which defence department did you report?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: The department of defence in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Did you report to any particular person in the department? Do you remember to whom you reported, the officer who was in charge, to whom you reported? I'm not interested in the name of the officer, but the position of the officer to whom you reported to the department of defence in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: All of us, all the refugees who came there to the department of defence in Busovaca, I mean I don't know all these people, and this was only my second day in Busovaca, so I did not know all these people. So, everyone reported in, and I reported in, too, and we were all given our assignments, and that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And after you reported, how long after you reported were you on your assignment?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't understand. What do you mean by when I reported to the department?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I'll make myself clear, I'll make my questions clear. You said you reported to the department of defence in Busovaca and after that you were given your assignment. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: How long after you reported were you given your assignment? How many days after you reported were you given your assignment?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, I reported that day and I cannot remember when I was given an assignment, the next day or the day after that. The most important thing is that I was given an assignment when I was needed by these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And were these assignments, this first assignment, was this first assignment given a day or two after you first reported, or could it have been given a week or a month after you reported to the department of defence?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, it wasn't a month after that. It was soon after that, because we were needed shortly. I can't remember after how many days, I know it wasn't a month, but I cannot remember how many days later it was. One day, two days, three days, perhaps five days at the most. That is when I had to go out and work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you were given the assignment; who gave you the assignment, and how were you notified of this assignment?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, when I reported to the defence department, they said you will be informed by the military police or by a messenger when you are needed. And that's the way it was. And I don't know exactly who this was, because I don't know all of these people exactly and who was, you know, in charge. I was a person who carried out certain work, and I do not remember exactly what date it was. It was simply that I carried out my duties according to this assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Pesa, I appreciate the fact that you did carry out your duties as a law abiding citizen. I do appreciate that. But my question to you is: Do you know, where were you when you were notified that you were to perform work duty? Were you at home or were you elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Sometimes I would be at home and sometimes I would be absent, because I'm a heavy smoker. I smoke a lot, so I didn't have any cigarettes so I would go to see a neighbour, someone else, to ask for a cigarette or two. Then when I would come home my wife would transmit all this information to me. She would tell me whether a messenger or the military police came looking for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So, there were occasions when you were at home when you were notified by a messenger or the military police.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, sometimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And on those occasions, on those times when you were at home, what form did this notification take? What was the form of the notification?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: "You, Mr. Anto Pesa, have been assigned to such and such a work duty." It was quite obvious where the secondary school was, where the collection centre was, and where we were supposed to report, so that is the kind of information I received.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So that person who came to your house would tell you that you, would ask you to identify yourself and then would say to you that you have to report at the secondary school at a specified time?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And he would say this to you orally.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And then you would accordingly go down and report to, near the secondary school in Busovaca, as you said.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you also said that, in answer to my learned friend, you said there were times about 15 to 20 people would report at the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And what would happen when you reported at the secondary school you were asked to report to?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: What do you mean what would happen? We would go there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And at that point would anybody talk to you or would you just -- what were you told to do at this collection point?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, we would meet there, 15, 20, 25 people, I cannot tell you exactly how many, and then the people who would come would say, "Well, go out for your work duties." And then we knew what our military duties were, we were supposed to go up there, and then there's a commander of the front line who would say, "you're supposed to dig here and there," et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And you said you would be accompanied, you were escorted to this place by either truck or tractor, and you would be escorted by the military police; am I right?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Who was the commander of your work unit, Mr. Pesa?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: I don't know exactly. Because I'm a refugee and I was not interested in who the commander was. I know what my military duty is, I wasn't interested in that. Where all my people went, that is where I went. You know, in the domain of what I was supposed to do. I wasn't interested at all in who the commander was. I was interested in doing my share of the work and whether we would come back alive and whether we would get wounded or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So you had no occasion to speak to the commander of a work unit?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you that at that point I was a refugee in Busovaca. I left my good land back there, I left my home and hearth there. I left my home and I came to unknown surroundings, and I was not interested in who was who, and who did what. I was interested in whether my children would remain alive, whether I would remain alive and whether I would manage to feed them. And I was not interested at all in who the commander was and who did what. I know that I was a military age man up to the age of 65, and I wanted to do my share of this work, and I didn't want anyone to have any problems with me, and I wasn't interested in anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I appreciate all that, but my question is whether you had an occasion to speak to the commander of your work unit, whether you had the opportunity to speak to the commander of your work unit.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And at this collection --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I withdraw that question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: You said you were taken to dig trenches in various locations, at any one of these locations were you beaten or maltreated or inhumanely treated while digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: No, no, I was never beaten, I was never mistreated, nor was I ever inhumanely treated. Not only I, but no one else was treated this way. We ate what there was to eat, we would smoke as many cigarettes as we had, we had breaks in our work, things were normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: So, you were treated quite well, and very correctly?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Yes, yes, towards me and towards everyone else. I mean, in this place where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And when you concluded your work duty assignment, you were brought back home, returned home in the same way, either by tractor or by truck.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: We would get down, I mean, we would walk through the forest to the place where the first vehicles would come, and then we would take these trucks and go home to get some rest, whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And more or less this was the procedure on all occasions that you were taken out on assignment.

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Well, yes. We would be taken by truck for as far as the truck could go, and we would go back the same way. That's the way it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And on none of those occasions did you have the opportunity or the occasion to speak to the commander of your work unit?

utterances.speaker: ANTO PESA.
utterances.text: Sir, I repeat the same word three times, I was not interested in who was what. I was interested in my own problems. I wanted to get my work done, and I was wondering what I would have for lunch that day and whether I would have any lunch. I did not know people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Meddegoda. Mr. Mikulicic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Pesa, the Trial Chamber has no questions for you. Thank you very much for coming to testify before this International Tribunal. We wish you a safe journey home. Thank you very much, Mr. Pesa. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, will it be possible to hear all the remaining witnesses today? Are the other witnesses here today? It seems that it is the case. If we are able to work quickly and efficiently, it seems we might be able to finish the testimony of the different witnesses that are left today. I think there are three witnesses left for this morning. I think that after hearing each witness we could take a break, since we have a lot of time before us. Let us take a 20-minute break and then we will hear the testimony of the second witness, and then we will take another break, and finally, the Trial Chamber will answer the questions that were put to the Trial Chamber during the status conference. The Trial Chamber has drawn up a number of proposals, so if we can use our time efficiently, I think we may have the time to finish our work today. We will now take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Sorry if we're a bit late. I have just learned, or rather, I was reminded of the fact that Mr. Mikulicic wishes to tender a number of documents, so we may have to extend today's hearing a little bit. We have received the interpreter's agreement. We have received the technician's agreement. So, if necessary, maybe we'll work until 2.30 this afternoon. But that will mean that tomorrow we would all be free. That would be our reward for working hard today. Do we all agree on this proposal? It seems that that is the case. It's nice to see that everybody is cooperating. Thank you very much for your cooperation. There are a number of things that we can talk about during the status conference, also. So, Mr. Mikulicic, maybe we can continue with the testimony of your witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence calls witness Mato Tavic to the stand

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tavic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now take your oath. The usher is holding out the text for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You may sit down, Mr. Tavic. Do you feel comfortable, Mr. Tavic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now answer the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Tavic.

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I am the Defence attorney in this hearing. I am going to ask you some questions. Would you please answer them to the best of your ability? Mr. Tavic, tell us when and where you were born?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I was born in the village of Maljine of the Municipality of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When were you born?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In 1935. What was the date?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: On the 12th of February, 1935.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tavic, what are you by nationality?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I am a Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That is your faith. What is your ethnic group, your nationality?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I am a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tavic, did you go to school?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: No. I went to two classes, the war was ongoing and my parents were not able to send me to school. We were all pilfered at the time and I had to fend for myself. I had to tend to the sheep and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, unfortunately, you were not able to continue your schooling after the second class of primary school?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Tavic, that you were born in the village of Maljine, near Travnik. How far is the village away from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: It's 12 kilometres away from Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you live your entire life in that village until the war, or anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Only in Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Have you got a family?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes. I have seven children. Jela is my eldest, she was born in 1959. 1960 (sic) is the second one, 1961. Mladen was born in 1977. Elza was born in 1978, Vijeko in 1974. So seven children in all (sic).

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understood you correctly, Mr. Tavic, you have four sons; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And three daughters?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Three daughters, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did you all live together in the Village of Maljine?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You had your own house there?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, I had three houses. One was destroyed. I have a picture of that house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have a picture of your house here with you?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, the new house. I had just lived in it for two years, and unfortunately I spent five years in Busovaca with my family.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any land, livestock?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, I had everything. I had 180 sheep. I had two cows. I had two horses, pigs. I had a Hungarian dog who listened to me more than my children. I had two other dogs as well, mountain dogs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any land, Mr. Tavic?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, more than 200 dulums.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say 200 dulums, that's about 200.000 square metres; is it not?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, if you can understand, jutro is ten dulums, five dulums, and one hectar is ninety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, it's a large plot of land, it's a large area of land?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, it is, particularly for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tavic, you were a fairly rich farmer, you had a lot of land and property?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, I was born in 1935, I did not work anywhere. I was a sort of builder. But I took some sheep, I was given a credit, a loan, and I had to fend for myself for all the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened, Mr. Tavic, in the first half of 1993 with your family and with your land, your property?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: My family went to Busovaca with me, and I have my eldest son who is still in Serbia, he is still imprisoned there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, one son was taken prisoner during the war by the Yugoslav People's Army and is still captive in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And your other three sons and your daughters lived together with your grandchildren in the village of Maljine, all together?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Why did you have to leave the village of Maljine?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Because we were expelled, we were driven out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who drove you out?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: The BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The army, you mean?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You gathered your family together and you all went together to Busovaca as refugees?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you find any lodging in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, I found an empty house in Busovaca. And my daughter also found an empty house, because she has her husband and two children and she also found temporary lodging, temporary shelter. And my son, Vinko did, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And so you remained in Busovaca until the present time?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tavic, when you came to Busovaca, what did your sons do? Did they report anywhere?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: They were in the HVO and still are. And as one of my neighbours who took me in asked me to cover a shed for him and bring hay to the shed and he would bring me milk in the morning, and I was ashamed, I tried to do something. And Tomo Julijanovic came up from Guca Gora. I asked him, "Where did you go?" And I said, "I was sent by the police," because they wanted my records, information on me, where I come from, what I do and so on. And then I went back home to my wife. Her name is Milka, and I said, "Melka, I must go and report," because I never wanted anybody else to come and make me, compel me to do so. I did so voluntarily. Vujica Andjelko is who I went to. I went to the municipality to report, and it was by the secondary school. There was a collection point there with the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tavic. Let's give the interpreters a chance to clarify matters. I'll take it question by question and then you can answer me. It will be easier that way. Let's go back to the events that you just mentioned. If I remembered you correctly, a neighbour in Busovaca asked you to put tiles, to repair his tile roof on his shed. And that neighbour, on the occasion, gave you some milk for helping him out and some food; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you did not have your own food, your own milk or food at the time?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: No, we didn't, that's right. We had some foodstuff, but not enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So there was a shortage of food?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, well, yes, it was wartime, so there were shortages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tavic, you said that another neighbour of yours came by, Tomo Julijanovic, and what did that neighbour tell you?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: He said he was taken by the police and that he had to say how old he was. And he went to his own home, I came back to my own home, and I reported on the next day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did Toma Julijanovic, your neighbour, say why the police came to interrogate him?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, they came to question him to see whether he could become part of an organisation, a civil defence organisation and civil protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And so from what you learned from Tomo Julijanovic, your neighbour, you got to know that you were expected to report. And where did you go to report?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I went to report to the municipality for civil defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the Busovaca municipality; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you mentioned another name, Vujica Andjelko; didn't you?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You contacted that man, you reported to him?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who was he? What did he do?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, he was the commander of that civil defence department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what did he tell you? Where did he assign you to?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: He asked me how old I was. I told him. I said I was a builder by profession, and then he gave me my assignment to dig trenches, and I would go and dig trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We've been asked, Mr. Tavic, to speak a little more slowly for the interpreters. So let's try and do that. My next question, Mr. Tavic, that man, Vujica Andjelko, told you that you had been given an assignment to a work unit, and he told you that you would have to go and work somewhere?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How did you know on what day you were to take up your assignment? Were you informed in some way?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, we were informed. For example, we would say, they would tell us today we would go to a work unit, and they would say, "You come the next day". Now, if I turned up and there was some shelling, then I would have to build up and clear up the region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Tavic, let's go back to the first part of your answer. Would somebody come to your house to inform you of when you should turn up for your assignment?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who would tell you where to report?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, in the evening of one day a policeman would tell us when to take up our shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, a military policeman informed you when to take up your shift and report for duty, report for work duty?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where would you then go in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: It was the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you would go to the secondary school, and other people to go on the same work unit would gather there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many people, approximately, made up one of those work units?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, sometimes, depending on need, 26, for example. Sometimes 17. It depended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you given any tools to work with?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, axes and shovels, picks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how were you taken to the localities? Were you transported?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes. There was a vehicle. We would get in and the policeman would get in with us and he would take us to the soldier there on the spot who would be with us while we dug the trenches. Later on, it was near the frontline, and if they wanted us to dig they would shoot, open fire on us. And he would send us back then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, once you had gathered in front of the secondary school, you were taken by some vehicle near the locality where you were to do your digging; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you escorted by the military police?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you reached the locality, who did you report to on the spot?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, we reported to a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The commander that was in charge of that area?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And did the commander tell you what to do and where to do it?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, he would tell us everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I understand. What did you do most often? What kind of work did you do most often up by the frontline?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, we would dig trenches, mostly trenches, and dugouts. And we looked for things to cover these dugouts and trenches with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tavic, did you do this work at night mostly, or during the day?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Always during the night, mostly during the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long would your shift last?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: We would go out around 9 p.m. and come back at 4 o'clock in the morning, just before dawn.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you given any food?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes. Just as the soldiers did, we got the same food as the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tavic, the localities where you did your digging, do you recall their names?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, I know Prosje was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any others?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I remember Polom, I remember Kula, and I also remember Podjele and Strane. And the village of Loncari.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Those were the localities, then, where you went digging, where your work unit was located. Can you tell us, please, how many times you went trench digging?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I can't quite remember, but three times. Three times to Prosje. Then I went to Podjele after that, once or twice. Then I went to Polom about four times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, all together, you went some 10 to 12 times; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Tavic, in addition to this trench digging, you also did some other work. You said you were a builder, a mason, and that you were able to use these skills when there was the shelling of a building and a building was shelled, then you would go and work there to build the building up again?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you recall where in Busovaca you did this building work?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, behind the municipal building, up towards Kadica Strane. I can't quite remember, I am getting a bit old. But I know it was somewhere in that region.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, you restored the school and the municipal building that had been destroyed by the shelling. Where are those buildings located in Busovaca, in the centre or in the suburbs?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: The school is in the centre of town. And the municipal building is in the centre of town, Kadica Strana Tisovacka 2, that is a little further away from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you do this building work frequently when buildings were destroyed by shelling in the town of Busovaca? Was that a frequent occurrence?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Busovaca was frequently shelled?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, it was, frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned, Mr. Tavic, that while you were digging trenches along the frontline that you were shot at?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, that's true, because sometimes they would hear us at night, because I would use my pick or axe and I would hit a stone, and then the enemy would hear us and they would open fire. And then we would be quiet for a little while and we saw that it was getting light, and they would send us back home.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you say they, who do you mean? The military police or somebody else?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: No, not the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who stood guard while you did the digging?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: The commander. He was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did some of your colleagues who dug together with you, was anybody ever wounded or killed during the work you did?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, on one occasion Puseljaj Niko hit a mine and he was killed on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have any weapons when you performed your work?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: No. Nobody could have had any arms, nobody did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just tools for digging?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the food like that you were given?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, the same, not enough, but just like the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the food like in Busovaca? The civilian population, what did they have to eat?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, if the people, those who had more food ate that, and they would give us food, the people who didn't. And I helped everybody, I always worked, so everybody gave me some food. I would be ashamed of this and then I would return the favour by doing some work for them, because I had a large family, I had to survive somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What other work did you do in the work unit, apart from digging trenches and building up these shelled buildings? What else did you do?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, I went to the mediapan factory and used sandbags for the fortifications of the buildings there. And I would do some cleaning work as well. That's where I worked the longest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tavic, while you dug trenches, did you notice near you or with you, some Muslims from Kaonik working?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: No, I didn't see anybody. And I don't know where Kaonik is, but nobody of that kind worked with me. They were just Croats. There are some Muslims in Busovaca now, but they did not go to the work units, and they're still living there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that Croats worked with you in your unit; does that mean within the composition of your work unit that your work unit was only composed of Croats, or were there some other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: There were some Serbs there, as well, and they remained there through mixed marriage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tavic, you said you've never been to Kaonik; do you know what exists in Kaonik, what kind of facility?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I heard there was a prison there, but I never went there. I'm afraid of prisons. I was never detained, not one single hour or one single day, never detained in my life.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Tavic, what do you do in Busovaca now? How do you make a livelihood?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, I am working in the utilities. I am a dustman. I collect garbage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever go back to your native village and see your house?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, for the first time when I saw what had become of my house, with the old house and with the new sort of weekend house, I was astounded with the fate that had befallen us. And I have a photograph of the new house. I took a photograph, and I have the picture with me. The house is now completely in ruins, completely destroyed. I have a picture of my new place. And I never go again, because when I go it's very upsetting. I have to be given injections and take pills to calm me down. So I don't like going there. I went on the 7th of August once when a man called Adem Zarkic came out of Jajce, and he told me that -- (inaudible), and I thought that my house is a happy house, that nothing would happen to it. But, unfortunately, my house was completely destroyed. All the installations were pulled out. Everything has been ruined in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So there is nothing of the property you once had?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Just one house, if you want to see it, a picture of it. I have three sons. Each of them would like to go back to their native village, but they have nowhere to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: May we ask the usher to place the photo on the ELMO? Is that the house that you're talking about, Mr. Tavic? And that house was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We can remove the photograph now. Mr. Tavic, you said you lived in the village of Maljine; didn't you? Do you remember who was your neighbour? What family was the neighbouring family near your house? Who lived there?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, my neighbours also lived in Tavic, and the village of Maljine was populated by Muslims, and we were Croats. And we respected each other as friends, as neighbours. And suddenly what happened happened, and this changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tavic, who was your Muslim neighbour who lived near your house? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Dautovic Vehad was my neighbour, Mr. Dautovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, the Dautovic family; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you know Hamdo Dautovic?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, that's my neighbour. Of course I do, he is my neighbour, but he is a little lower down. Nedzo and Osman is closer to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Hamdo Dautovic was your neighbour; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What kind of a man was he, Mr. Tavic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I object to...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, you're right, Mr. Niemann. Mr. Mikulicic, could we please remove that detail?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tavic, let me just ask you one more question. When you were digging trenches along the frontline, did you see soldiers of the Croatian army, the HV soldiers there, or did you see any soldiers of the HVO, the Croatian Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I don't recall seeing anybody, just in Busovaca. People know me in Busovaca, but I forget people because I am getting on in age.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I understand, Mr. Tavic. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Niemann, Mr. Meddegoda. No, Mr. Niemann, I see. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Mr. Tavic, during 1992, did you work on your property as a farmer during that year or did you do up some other form of work? That's the year before you went to Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I worked on my own land with my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you arrived at Busovaca and you found out that you were required to carry out civilian work, you readily volunteered to do this work, I take it?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, at no stage did any policeman ever threaten you or threaten to put you in jail or anything like that? As soon as you found out this was your duty, you went voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the frontline to dig these trenches, did it ever happen that anyone had to force you to work there? I mean, did police ever point guns at you and threaten you or do anything like that when you were there? Or did you just work voluntarily?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: No, voluntarily. I went voluntarily. Nobody ever forced me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And I think you said, when you were giving your evidence a minute ago, that when you were at the frontline, did the commander took over, the military commander took over at that stage; did he?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes. He would take us over, yes, and he'd take care of us. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And did the policeman that took you there, did he withdraw and go back to the vehicles or something; did he? The policeman that brought you there?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: He would withdraw. He would go back to his command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what month it was that you actually got to Busovaca in 1993? Do you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: The beginning, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So, in the early part of 1993?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, when you had a work unit, either when you went to dig trenches or you did any other sort of work, was there somebody who was in charge of your unit? Did you have a commander of your particular unit, or was it always just the military commander who told you what you should do?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: When I was repairing buildings that were shelled, Ivica Bartulovic was the commander, and he would tell us what we were supposed to do when we'd go to that house. And we would do what he told us to do and then we'd go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Was he a policeman or a military man or just a civilian like yourself?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: A plain civilian.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You don't happen to know any of the names of the military commanders that you worked for when you were digging trenches by any chance?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: I don't know any one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Now, you dug trenches at nighttime and that was because it was safer, you couldn't be seen as easily during the nighttime?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: And indeed, even during the night, if the firing got too strong from the other side, you would retreat back from the frontline; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Mato Tavic
utterances.text: Yes, we would.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, any further questions you would wish to put to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence doesn't have any further questions. We just have something to say in terms of the interpretation, the transcript, page 52, line 2. In the transcript it says that the witness worked on the land with his father, but he actually said that he worked with sheep. It sounds almost the same in the Croat language, so... So I think that the transcript should be corrected in that sense. No further questions from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. I heard sheep myself, so I don't know if there has been, in fact, an interpretation problem in the English booth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: I have a question both for Mr. Niemann and Mr. Mikulicic. A photograph has been exhibited, from the technical point of view, shouldn't that be part of the record of the Court?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your Honours, I am not pressing that it be tendered. I didn't want, and strictly speaking there could be an argument of its relevance, but under the circumstances it's not something that I wanted to raise, and I don't mind which way it's dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence did not intend to tender this photograph as evidence because we simply did not know that the witness would show this photograph. He carries it with him as a momento, so he showed it to us, but we had no intention of tendering it as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: As for myself, I think it was something rather emotional for the witness, and I always think that the witnesses should be allowed to express their feelings. I did have the impression that it was a very emotional situation for the witness, so I think that this exhibit should be tendered.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Judge Rodrigues, the picture that was put on the ELMO, we can make a copy of this picture, thanks to the video recording of this hearing. It is not a problem, the witness can keep the photograph, we can make a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: That won't be necessary. I don't think it will be necessary. We all agree on the fact that, in fact, the Defence did not wish to tender the exhibit. It was only something that the witnesses wanted to bring up. We don't need, I think, to make a copy of this picture. Mr. Tavic, it's the presiding judge addressing you. The Trial Chamber has no further questions for you. Thank you very much for coming. We wish you a safe journey home. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. (The witness withdrew)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
