utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, Mr. Niemann, I think it is a good time to take a fifteen minute break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Mr. President, I apologise for coming in late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No problem, Mr. Dubisson, we accept your apologies. All right, let us resume our work. I forgot to mention something before the break. Mr. Mikulicic, allow me to address Mr. Aleksovski directly. Mr. Aleksovski, would you please stand? Due to your health problems, is it possible for you to follow the hearing until 2.30, or is that a problem for you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you. For the entire time I have felt your care and attention towards me in the sense of my health. I feel well. I am a little moved; but, of course, I would like us to move forward as fast as possible and get through as much work as possible. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Aleksovski. All right, then we can continue, Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. The Defence calls witness Dusan Lukovic to the stand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: (The witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukovic. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: You will now take the oath. The usher is holding out the text for you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you. You may take your seat. For the moment being, I will ask you to answer the questions put to you by Mr. Mikulicic. Mr. Mikulicic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Lukovic. As Defence attorney, I would like to ask you some questions. Please answer them to the best of your ability. I should also like to ask you that when answering that you bear in mind that you should speak slowly so that the interpreters can keep up with your statements and with my questions, thank you. Mr. Lukovic, tell us when and where you were born.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I was born in 1935, in Banja Luka. By vocation I am professor of sociology. I am now retired. I have been retired since the 1st of May, 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On what date were you born?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: 22nd of September 1935, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, what are you by nationality?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Are you a believer?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I am an atheist.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Lukovic what schooling you have had?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I finished teachers' school and faculty of political science in Sarajevo, the sociology stream.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, by profession, you graduated as a sociologist and you are a professor of sociology?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you serve in the former Yugoslav Peoples Army?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Yes, I did serve the army in Novi Sad in 1935 and 1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After your military service, did you receive a rank?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I went to a course for -- I was a lance corporal, and later on I became a sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: They are all non-commissioned officers?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Yes, because I did not complete the school for officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, can you tell us where you worked and what position you held?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: For 40 years, I lived in Vitez. And I performed many jobs during that time. I am going to quote just some of them because there were many of them. I was director of the popular university, which is an education institution for adults and for cultural activity in my municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just a little slower, please.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: After that I was director of the secondary school centre, which is an institution for education, which encompasses secondary schools and gymnasiums. After that, I was the director of the work community of self-protection and information. This is an institution which covered the whole, the three military companies, the one in Princip Seljo, for production purposes, the production of explosives; and Sintevit, which produced plastics. This firm did this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Lukovic, let's move tacitly without entering into detail. Did you hold any political functions?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: For four years I was the vice-president of the municipal assembly or vice-mayor of Vitez, then I was the president of the municipal assembly of Vitez on two occasions in 1983 and 1984, my first time term of office, and 1985 the second term. And as the president of the municipal assembly in Vitez in 1985 I was president of the community of municipalities of Travnik, Novi Travnik and Vitez. This was a volunteer function because I still perform my duties as mayor of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From what you have just told us, Mr. Lukovic, may we conclude that you were a distinguished and prominent citizen in Vitez and its environs?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Well, it will be a little immodest, but I must say I was, of Zenica, Travnik, Busovaca and all that part, because we had a lot of cooperation with the republic itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, where did you find yourself in mid-1993 with the start of the war operations?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I have been living in Vitez since 1958; therefore, I was in Vitez at the time in my flat with my wife, with my son and his wife, and with my grandchild.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you live in your own house or do you live in an apartment building?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I do not have my own house, I live in an apartment building, and I live in a flat which I got when I worked in the factory. I was given the flat for my accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You say that you lived in your flat at the time with your wife, with your son and his wife and your grandchildren?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, how did you experience those days, the first hostile incidents between the Croats and Muslims in the area?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Well, the first thing that we noted was the attack by the planes of the Yugoslav Peoples Army. There were two bombardments on the occasion. One was the military factory was attacked. That was one target. First of all, they missed it, but on the second occasion there was panic because part of the factory was destroyed. When the war began on the 16th of April, if I remember correctly, in 1993, the situation was very tense. There was a lot of shooting. There was shelling. Explosions could be heard, sporadic explosions, and there was general psychological tension. And people would go down into the basement to take shelter. They were safer in the basements. That was at the beginning, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Lukovic, that there was some shelling, the shelling of Vitez took place. Who shelled Vitez?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Vitez was shelled by the members of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, from the Muslim regions. And the shells, the grenades fell even near the flat where I lived. Two buildings were severely damaged, and the flat in which I, myself, lived, all the glass broke. The windows broke. And it was very lucky that my grandchildren were not killed. They were injured, however. These metal parts went through the flat and they were injured. And also the walls were destroyed and the cupboards were pierced where our clothes were hanging, and it landed under the bed, and my wife happened to be in the bedroom at that time. There was more shelling, as well, so that in a section not far from the centre of town eight children were killed, and there is a monument to those children there today. There were cases where a child was killed on the street, where a father was feeding his son and the child was killed in his arms. And the military first aid centre was also shelled, as was the popular university in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Can we then conclude that in the area of the town itself and the surrounding areas there was no place of safety, no place that was not shelled?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Well, I talked to my friends, as well, what they meant by the frontline where the shooting took place. I think that the whole of Vitez was the frontline. There was danger everywhere. And I'll say something about this later on. I felt myself to be safer along the frontlines where I went digging trenches and dugouts. I felt safer there than in Vitez proper, apart from Bombasi, which was one particular locality which was a little safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, you have just started a topic, which I should like to discuss at greater length, and that is your involvement during those war days of 1993, your work responsibilities, work duties. Could you describe to us how you took part in the work that you did?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I did not report on a voluntary basis. I was 60, and by law I was a recruit, a military-aged man. I know this from earlier on, because as president I commanded the exercise, training situations that we had which were called steel 83. So I knew what a conscript meant and the military age of men. And one morning the military police came to my door, they rang the bell very nicely, I opened the door, they said, "Are you Lukovic Dusan?" I said, "Yes, that's me," and they told me urgently to report to the public library. They said thank you and they left. They said it was urgent. I went to the library, I found people there that I knew. I think there was a man called Males, he was a courier, and another man, Stipinovic, I think was also a professor of sociology. And they told me that I was, by law, to report to a work unit, assigned to a work unit. And I was told the kind of work that I would be expected to do. So, I was always informed by courier. The courier was the military police, because under conditions of war it is very difficult to write written requests and invitations, and then 24 hours had to expire, which were the regulations beforehand. But it was the military police that would come and call us, and we would collect at the collection points and were then told what to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, you turned up at the designated time, the military police had told you it was your duty to comply with that, and you were then told that you would be joining a work unit; is that right?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you describe to us, Mr. Lukovic, the procedure? How were you sent to the locality for your work duties? What was the collection point? Who escorted you to the locality and who gave you your work orders?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Well, we would gather at several locations. The first place I went to was the library, municipal library, where a mini-bus would come and collect us and take us to the, as near to the locality as possible, then we would go on foot. In this case it was a mountain with a little weekend house there, and we would go to perform our work duties there. There was a Muslim attack several days prior to this, and then we had to extend the trenches and the dugouts and fox holes and see to the general fortification of the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did anybody escort you in the mini-bus, or did you go on your own?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: The driver of the mini-bus was told to escort us to the locality and to bring us to the unit and the commander of the frontline, and so you would contact that commander then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did the commander give you any instructions as to what your work duties would be?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: When I arrived on the scene, the commander would inform us of why we had come and what our work was to be, what our work would involve. The tools were already there, axes, picks, shovels, axes and so on. This was the frontline, and he would explain to us where we were located from the aspects of the other forces, where the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina was located, where the danger points were. They told us where to dig and that we shouldn't move around because a sniper could hit us at any time, that it was a danger area. So we were told about the terrain, our work duties and the dangers involved and how we were protected. And as we were digging there were members of the HVO present with weapons, they were there to ensure safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many people made up your work units, Mr. Lukovic?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Well, I worked in several localities, in different work units, so that the number was different each time. When we were in Zabrdze there were between 15 and 20 of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how many times were you taken on this work assignment?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Well, to Zabrdze, there is a village called Zaselje in Bobasi where the situation was the most difficult. Lazine, or the village of Tulovici, Baringaj, that is above Ahmici; and those are the work units where I worked physically. And then in November 1993 I received a written request from the civilian protection unit, and from the armed forces I entered the civilian protection units and worked other guards posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: The witness is speaking of events of November of 1993, which is clearly outside the ambit of the indictment, Your Honours, and I think Mr. Mikulicic himself has objected to the Prosecution leading evidence outside of May of 1993 on a number of occasions, and it is on the same basis that I object to the witness's answers being elicited outside of the period of the indictment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, I don't think it is as necessary to go beyond the dates that are covered by the indictment. You may continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I say something at this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Defence fully respects the objection of the Prosecution and does not wish to step outside the frameworks of the indictment; but sometimes the witness spontaneously speaks about a time outside the indictment. But the Defence will remain within the frameworks of the indictment and will not pose questions outside that framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Yes, we also understand that the witness has launched on a number of events that are not covered on the indictment. Let us go back to the dates that are covered in the indictment, please. Witness, do you want to say something? Please, speak freely.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wanted to say that as I was in the work units for one year, and in speaking I stepped over the framework of the time frame of the indictment, so I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: No problem. Mr. Mikulicic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Lukovic, you have understood that in your statement we are going to be moving within a single time framework and we're not going to be going out of it, so that is roughly the first half of 1993. All right. You said on several occasions as a member of the work unit, you dug trenches, dugouts, et cetera; how much time would you approximately spend at a given location during your work duty?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Either one day or two days, three days, 15 days, 18 days, and even outside this limit. About two-and-a-half to three months we were digging trenches, with interruptions, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Lukovic, what was the ethnic composition of these work units? What ethnic groups were in the work units? Were they different or was it a single one?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I am talking about the work unit I was in, myself, where I worked, myself. Not a single one of these work units, though, belonged to a single ethnic group. There were Serbs, Croats, Muslims, even Slovenes, because in Vitez there are even Slovenes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Lukovic, when doing this work, were you provided with food, accommodation and things like that?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: There was a war going on, the terrain itself was rather complicated, and I said in the beginning we had transportation, and also we had food provided for us, because we had three meals when we worked. We ate the same food that the soldiers of the HVO had. Now, whether we had accommodation, well, it wasn't really very adequate accommodation. These were weekend cottages that were devastated, that were damaged. And we also stayed in houses that could be used. So, I think that accommodation was appropriate, because we had blankets, and where there was no proper floor we had hay, but we did have accommodation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us, Mr. Lukovic, how was your safety organised, I mean, for all of you who were digging out there?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Our safety was provided for by virtue of the fact that on the same frontline we were at, there were armed soldiers, and they never left us. And they were there, of course, vigilant, as vigilant as could be. I don't know how it was at other positions. They would even tell us when to duck so that snipers could not get us. And then Zabrdze, we stayed for another day, and we were told we had to stop working at one o'clock, and we asked why. And they said that they had received information that they should expect an attack by the BH army. So we all left our tools, and five armed members of the HVO with automatic rifles in front of us took us to a safe place, and then we took buses to Vitez from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you remember any occasion when somebody actually got wounded or killed?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: At Bobasi we worked at night. And we urgently had to dig trenches and fox holes, and the Muslims started their offensive in the morning. They opened fire. And two Muslims and one Croat who worked there was killed by a sniper. And we also had another occasion at Barin Gaj, this above Ahmici. I think this person was called Zrnic, Anto Zrnic. He wasn't careful enough. He was showing where his house was, where his village was, and I was there when a young soldier said, "Don't stand there, a sniper can get you." And I went about 80 metres away from there, we were supposed to make a dugout out of a trench, and I was informed afterwards that he had to take care of a dead body. He was killed, but he wasn't killed immediately. He died in the vehicle that he was taken to afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What ethnic group did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the food that you received at the frontline. Tell me, what was this food like? Was it sufficient for your needs? Or was this food insufficient?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Well, you know, that is relative. I was a man whose weight was about 806 (sic) kilograms at that time. And before the war, when the war broke out and when I started digging trenches, I lost weight. I weighed only 86 kilograms. Also all the members of my family lost weight because there wasn't enough food and it wasn't very high calorie food, and we ate all the food that the soldiers ate, absolutely the same food. We even sat together and ate together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Now, Mr. Lukovic in the transcript, that the number of kilograms, how many kilos did you weigh?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I lost 20 kilograms, because I weighed 106 kilograms and my weight went down to 86 kilograms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have a son, Mr. Lukovic; don't you?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did your son do at that time?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: My son has a degree in law. He is a Serb by nationality, and he was a military-aged man, a conscript, and he had weapons. He was armed, a military man. And he was there at that frontline from the beginning until the end. And he was also wounded at one of these points, because they were shooting with RPGs, and he was in that trench. His right arm was wounded, two metal fragments were taken out of his hand. I am trying to say that he is a disabled person now, 30 per cent disabled, and he even gets a disablement pension.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, excuse me for interrupting; but, again, I think there is some confusion as to the weight of the witness. What I have heard in the French interpretation is that Mr. Lukovic weighed 106 kilograms, he lost 20 kilograms during the war; therefore, he later on weighed 86 kilograms. The transcript says that he lost 120 kilos, that's totally impossible. I think that we need to clear up the matter. Mr. Lukovic weighed 106 kilograms, he lost 20 kilograms and ended up weighing 86 kilograms. I hope I am right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour. Thank you for your intervention. I must say that I did not notice this disproportion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, just one clarification, please. Your son, your son fought in armed units, you mentioned it, but you did not say what army.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: In the armies of the HVO, of the Croatian Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay, that is clear now. And you said that he was wounded and he became a disabled person. Tell me, Mr. Lukovic, when you were digging at the frontline, when you were out there, did anybody mistreat you? Did anybody physically abuse you, beat you or anything?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Vitez is a small municipality, you know, and everyone knows one another. And I lived there for a long time, and we know all each other well. Perhaps there were certain incidents that I didn't hear of, one or two, perhaps. I heard of one, and I intervened there. Nobody forced us to work exhaustingly. We worked as much as we could. But, you know, I am the type, I worked very hard, and I was even spurring the other Croats and Muslims who were there to work faster; because we would keep our young people alive that way. And UNPROFOR would come in, if we managed to have well fortified lines, and then there would be negotiations. So I was never mistreated, nor any of the people who were with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said, Mr. Lukovic, that you did not volunteer into these work units?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: No, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And tell me, now, when you think about all of this, when this work duty, when you think of this work duty, how do you interpret this work duty?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Well, you see the war broke out, and I experienced war as a child; and in this war, it was difficult to decide that you would go to the frontline and dig trenches when your son is on the frontline, when your wife and children, grandchildren are at home. But since I was president, I knew what the national defence was and I knew how important this was and what kind of duty and responsibility this was. I was not 60 years old, and I knew that I was a military-aged man and that I would have to answer this call up, because that is what the law says. And of course I accepted this as a loyal citizen, as a military-aged man. And I think I honourbly carried out this duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony, Mr. Lukovic. The Defence has no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Mikulicic. I think there is still a slight confusion. I think maybe the court reporters made the mistake this time. But what I have said a moment ago does not appear clearly in the transcript. So, can we clear the matter once and for all? I hope the mistakes made in the transcript can be corrected. Again, I repeat, the witness weighed 106 kilograms. 106 kilograms. He lost 20 kilos, 2-0. And he, therefore, weighed 86 kilograms, 8-6. Right. We got it right this time. Mr. Meddegoda, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, when you volunteered for work in the work units, you volunteered within the civilian protection department of the Vitez municipality; did you?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: First of all, I did not volunteer. And I think that I said that in my statement. I did not report to the civil protection, but the military police informed me that I was supposed to report at the city library, and that's exactly what I did. And later on I found out at the frontline that these were work units attached to HVO units. And as far as civil defence is concerned, they called me up much later. This was in November, but then I was on the work unit of the civil defence. But then I had weapons as a guard where I took care of trucks, and also there was a mortuary there because they would bring in dead soldiers, the Red Cross would bring in dead soldiers from the fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: When you reported to the library, that was the public library in the Municipality of Vitez; is it?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And was there a person in charge of your work unit? A commander of the work unit?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: At that time there were two persons employed. There was one person who was more of a messenger, and later on I found out that the commander of the work units was Vinac, that was his last name, and his first name was Marijan or Mirjan, I don't know exactly. He often took a mini-bus taking us to the frontline, and he would receive his orders from the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: And was he the commander of all the work units within the Vitez municipality, or was he only a commander of your work unit that you were attached to?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I cannot say for sure. You see, almost in every village, wherever necessary, work units were set up, depending on the positions and on the situation, on the ground. In my particular case, yes, I mean, the place where I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: As you said in your evidence, in the course of your evidence a while ago, you and all the others were mistreated or beaten while you were involved in trench digging and in fortification work?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I read this oath, and believe me that I am saying the truth. I am saying -- I am talking about what I experienced, and that is the only thing that I can give testimony about. I'll give you an example. When we were building, when we were digging in Barin Gaj, there was a captain who was there, and I knew him from the military factory where we worked together; he gave us his room to spend the night there, on the couch where I was sleeping, a Muslim man also slept. So I am just trying to say how friendly we all were. We were all friends. Of course we were confused by everything that was happening, but that is so difficult to understand, anyway. So, I am just trying to describe the situation to you as it was. We were not mistreated, there were not any problems, their attitude towards us was fair, and even sometimes the soldiers would put their weapons down and they would dig together with us. So, again, I said this was a multi-ethnic work unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have to correct the transcript. My question was neither you nor the others were mistreated, that was my question; but it has been recorded incorrectly. And for that reason, I would wish the transcript to be corrected. My question to the witness was that neither he nor the others, none of the other members of his work unit were mistreated or beaten during the time they engaged in their work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEDDEGODA
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, any further questions for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Defence has no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE VOHRAH
utterances.text: Professor, did I hear you right when you said that your son was of Serb nationality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO NAVIA
utterances.text: At that time, did you ever see soldiers of the Croatian army with the HV insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: In Vitez? I never did. And I think that it would be very difficult for members of the Croatian army to get to Vitez. For example, a part of Vitez is called Mahala, and it was surrounded by the Croats. All of Vitez on the other hand, was surrounded by the Muslims, that is the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So I did not see a single person who had HV on his sleeve, only HVO. These were young men who we knew who were practically locals. Perhaps there were some, but I never saw any such persons. I only heard later, also, that there were only HVO soldiers there. I mean those belonging to Central Bosnia, so Croats, but from Central Bosnia, as we say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, I will follow on the question put to you by Judge Nieto Navia. Were you familiar with the HVO and HV insignias?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: The HVO, yes; but the Croatian army, no, I didn't see this. But the HVO, on the left arm, I think, they had a chessboard, and it said HVO. I don't know if there was another insignia, but there was a chessboard and it said HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Another question. The HVO soldiers always wore the HVO insignias on their uniforms, or did it happen sometimes that they did not wear any insignia on their uniform?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: The ones I saw wore insignia. They even had a band. I don't know whether it would be red or blue, whatever, showing what unit they belonged to. But they all wore uniforms and they all had insignia, and we were without uniforms. But we were not civilians, we were military-aged men in civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I see. So you said you went to dig trenches on a different number of locations. When you went there, did you ever see prisoners from the Kaonik facilities?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: I did not see any at the places I was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Were you ever informed of the fact that some prisoners from Kaonik were used to dig trenches?

utterances.speaker: Dusan Lukovic
utterances.text: Personally I was not told about that. But then, I have heard until now that there were such things. There were some of our people who did make mistakes, and they would serve in a unit and they would perhaps make a mistake at the frontline and then disciplinary action would be taken against them, they would be detained for three days or five days. So I knew that there was this prison, which is only natural in a state of war. If there are military police and if mistakes are made. I mean, this is my opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Very well, Professor. I don't think we have any further questions for you. Thank you very much. We wish you a safe journey home. Thanks again for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, too. And I wish you the best of luck, as well. (The witness withdrew).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, maybe you could begin to introduce the documents you wish to introduce. Let us not cut our work short. If you agree with me, I think there is no need for a break right now. You may begin to introduce your documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before tendering these documents, I just want to check one fact. If Your Honours recall during the cross-examination of professor Bianchini, our expert, the defence tendered two exhibits as evidence; however, these documents were originally only in the Croatian language. And then the registry took upon themselves to have these documents translated, and then they would be included into evidence at that point. This has been done in the meantime. So, Your Honours, may we formally tender this as evidence now? And they have been registered as D7 and D11 respectively. And that is document D7, and document D11 is a letter from the embassy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, or rather, sorry, Mr. Niemann, have you had the opportunity to look at these documents? Do you have anything to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No objections, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, in that case, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, the Defence received from the Prosecution -- Your Honours, the Defence has received from the Prosecution certain documents which we would like to tender as evidence and these documents were handed over to the Defence at our own request, according to the Rules of Procedure on giving documents which could influence the position of the defendant. However, bearing in mind the documents that were provided by the Government of Croatia, provided that these documents are not published, are not out in the public and that they be not be given to a third person, a third party. Since the Defence was thus cautioned by the Prosecution, I wish to suggest, if my learned colleague agrees, that we move on to a closed session, so that we could tender these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have no objection if he wants to make a submission in closed session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: I will ask the technical booth to ensure that we are now in closed session. (In closed session)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES
utterances.text: 24 Recess taken at 12.40 p.m.
